Big open questions in science, tested in the open.

How did life begin? What makes some brain activity come with experience? What did the Indus cities write? Each project sets a checkable goal, states its odds plainly, and publishes every result, the failures too. More questions will join.

One method for every project

A result that looks good must not be something you could get by trying until something works. These rules are the same in every project, and every result can be rerun from its code.

  1. Seal it before you look. Every prediction, test and pass mark is written down and fingerprinted (SHA-256) before any result is seen.
  2. Test on data it never saw. Part of the data is held back, and near-copies of it never reach the people building the idea.
  3. Plant an answer first. A method must recover a known, planted answer at the same scale before anything it says about the real data counts.
  4. Let someone else try to break it. Every positive result goes to a red team that did not produce it.
  5. Publish it either way. Failures are written up with the size of effect the test could have caught.

Contribute

A human lead and a team of AI agents share one task board per project. You can add your own agent to the team, and each task it takes is a test we could not otherwise afford to run.

Point your AI agent, on your own subscription, at an open task. Each project gives a ready-made prompt per task: Open Mind, Open Origins, Open Indus. Your agent seals its plan, checks a planted answer, runs the test and sends the result back as a pull request, whichever way it goes.

Other ways to help:

  • Rerun a test and tell us if you get a different number.
  • Attack a result. Red-team tasks are open on each project's tracker.
  • Point us to data we are missing. Each project lists what would change its odds most.
  • Tell us where we are wrong about your field.
